name: Dimensional Homogeneity
description: The principle that you can only add/subtract quantities with the same units

content.overview: You wouldn't add 3 apples to 5 oranges and call it '8 fruit-apples,' right? Same logic applies here: you can't add meters to seconds. That rule has a name — dimensional homogeneity — and it's simpler than it sounds. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
This one's straightforward but it matters a lot. {{viz:diagram-02}}

**The rule: you can only add or subtract quantities that share the same dimensions. And both sides of an equation have to match dimensionally too.**

**What that looks like in practice:**

Totally fine: 5 meters + 3 meters = 8 meters ✓ (length + length)
Also fine: 10 seconds + 5 seconds = 15 seconds ✓ (time + time)

Not okay: 5 meters + 3 seconds = ??? ✗ (length and time don't mix)
Not okay: 10 kg + 5 m/s = ??? ✗ (mass plus velocity means nothing)

**Why does this rule even exist?**

Because physics equations are describing something real, and reality doesn't bend the rules. A distance is a distance. A time is a time. They just don't turn into each other.

So if you saw someone write: distance = speed + time

In dimension-speak, that's [L] = [L T⁻¹] + [T] — mixing velocity and time on the same side of an equals sign. That equation is broken before you even plug in numbers. {{viz:chart-01}}

**Compare that to one that works:**

**distance = speed × time**

Left side: [L]
Right side: [L T⁻¹] × [T] = [L]

They match — this equation checks out. {{viz:anim-01}}

**Same idea applies to adding things up:**

This is fine: **Total distance = distance₁ + distance₂ + distance₃** — every term is [L].

This is nonsense: **Total = distance + speed + mass** — you're mixing [L], [L T⁻¹], and [M], three completely different things.

**Your go-to checklist:**

1. Look at the equation
2. Write down the dimensions of every term
3. Make sure everything on the left matches everything else on the left
4. Same for the right side
5. Make sure left matches right
6. Any mismatch means the equation is wrong — no exceptions
keyPoints: You can only add or subtract quantities that share the same dimensions
Both sides of an equation must land on the same dimensions
You can't add meters + seconds, or kg + m/s — it just doesn't mean anything
This rule is called dimensional homogeneity
Use it as your go-to check for whether an equation makes sense
Mismatched dimensions always mean a wrong equation
content.whyItMatters: This is your last line of defense before trusting an equation. If the dimensions don't line up, you already know something's broken — no need to even crunch the numbers first.
